newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH STOCKS FALL AS INVESTORS AWAIT CROWN OUTCOME.
newsitem.headline: CZECH STOCKS FALL AS INVESTORS AWAIT CROWN OUTCOME.

text.p: Czech stocks fell sharply on Wednesday as the crown continued to gyrate and investor feared an official devaluation against the dollar-mark basket against which the currency is fixed. Dealers said prices would not rise significantly until the currency crisis was resolved.
The Prague Stock Exchange's main PX50 index closed down 2.63 percent or 12.9 points down at 476.7, its lowest since March 1996, as prices fell across the board.
Several stocks hit year-lows.

"We expect that there will be further selling pressure in blue chip stocks because it seems that the market is adjusting prices in expectation of a devaluation which could be 10 or 15 percent so prices should stabilise at these levels," said Miroslav Nosal, head of research at Patria Finance.

The crown floats within bands set by the central bank, with a 7.5 percent cent fluctuation from the parity value of its currency basket. The bank could either widen the bands or lower the mid point, dealers said. "We do not expect any stabilisation before the situation is resolved," he added.
Speculative short-selling of the crown, which began last week and led the central bank to sharply raise interest rates, have hit stock prices badly.
The PX50, which peaked this year at 627.7 on February 24, fell 2.8 percent on Tuesday and 1.1 percent on Monday.

"Some of the companies are starting to look attractive but I do not think prices will go substantially higher in the short term because there is so much uncertainty about the Czech crown," said trader Jan Sykora of Wood & Company.
Financial stocks were badly hit. Komercni Banka plunged 138 crowns to 1,632 by 1230 GMT and Zivnostenska Banka was down 124 at 2,356 crowns.
SPT Telecom stood 155 crowns lower at 2,850. Power generator CEZ bucked the trend, rising six crowns to 895.

"There is no-one that can buy on the market. The Czech players don't have any cash left...foreigners are ready to buy but they are not going to if there is a chance of a devaluation," said Dan Gladis, broker at Atlantik Financni Trhy in the eastern city of Brno.
Gladis said the crown crisis and accompanying sky-high interest rates were hurting the capital market, which has long been criticised for its opacity and lax regulation.

"They are damaging an already poor reputation and destroying relationships that people have built up," he said, adding that foreign investors were unwilling to borrow crowns at high prevailing rates to buy stocks.
He said the slump in stock prices was also hurting the economy and making it difficult for companies to raise capital.
"You won't have any serious business even in the good companies unless this situation is resolved," he said.
However, analysts said prices had fallen so low, they were reaching a level that investors may find hard to resist.
"This freefall probably is too deep, prices have fallen too much and I would say there is still fundamental value," said trader Karl Ruzicka of ING Barings.

Nosal said a devaluation, if it came despite the government and central bank's rejection of the idea, could help prices of export-focused companies. He highlighted cigarette maker Tabak, a unit of Philip Morris Cos , confectioner Cokoladovny and brewer Prazske Pivovary .
However, he said CEZ could suffer if interest rates remained higher after the crisis than before as this could restrict economic growth and electricity consumption.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
